text: A psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.
It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praise to your name, O Most High,
to declare your steadfast love in the morning and your faithfulness through the nights,
on the ten-stringed lute and on the harp, to the melody of the lyre.
For you have made me glad by your work, O LORD; at the deeds of your hands I sing for joy.
How great are your works, O LORD! How very deep are your thoughts!

versions.text: How great are your works, O LORD! How deep are your thoughts!
versions.explanation: The Hebrew מְאֹד ("very, exceedingly") intensifies the second line and is currently unrepresented; including it preserves the parallel escalation and adds rhythmic weight for oral reading.

text: The senseless one does not know, the fool does not understand this:
though the wicked spring up like grass and all evildoers blossom, they are doomed to destruction forever.
But you, O LORD, are on high forever.
For look at your enemies, O LORD, look: your enemies will perish; all evildoers will be scattered.
But you have lifted up my horn like that of a wild ox; I am anointed with fresh oil.
My eyes have looked in triumph on my foes; my ears have heard the doom of the evildoers who rise against me.

versions.text: My eye has looked down on those who lie in wait for me; my ears have heard the fate of the evildoers who rise against me.
versions.explanation: "Looked down on" in modern English idiom means "to despise/regard as inferior," which misrepresents the Hebrew sense of seeing one's watchful enemies defeated. Also "the fate of" is an interpretive addition; "doom" is closer to the elliptical Hebrew and reads more naturally aloud.

text: The righteous will flourish like the palm tree; they will grow tall like a cedar in Lebanon.
Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God.
They will still bear fruit in old age; they will stay fresh and green,
proclaiming that the LORD is upright: he is my rock, and there is no injustice in him.

versions.text: proclaiming that the LORD is upright: he is my rock, and there is no wrong in him.
versions.explanation: עַוְלָתָה denotes injustice or unrighteousness rather than the vaguer "wrong," and the more precise term sharpens the closing line.
